title: Needle weaving
subtitle: Thread woven over parallel foundation bars to make a detached woven filling or band
excerpt: Needle weaving is a surface embroidery technique in which a thread is woven over and under a set of parallel foundation threads without the needle entering the fabric. The result is a firm woven bar or filling that sits above the ground cloth. It is used for detached leaves, bands, and fillings in raised embroidery and pulled thread work.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), needleweaving and drawn thread work chapters (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), needleweaving entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: The parallel foundation threads laid first, over which the weaving thread passes. In needle weaving they are held only at their ends by the fabric; the weaving thread passes between them without piercing the ground cloth.

content.text: Needle weaving works like miniature hand weaving done on the surface of fabric. A set of

is laid as the foundation, and a weaving thread is passed over and under those threads in rows without the needle touching the fabric underneath. Each row packs down against the last, building a firm woven structure that can be shaped into bars, leaves, or fillings. A blunt tapestry needle is used for the weaving pass so the fabric threads are not split.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 3 to 6 strands for warp; 2 to 3 strands for the weaving thread, which can be the same colour or contrasting

items.label: Needle 1
items.value: Embroidery needle size 7 for laying warp threads

content.text: Lay the warp threads: bring the thread up at point (A) at one end of the shape, carry it across to point (B) at the other end, and take it down. Bring it up very close to (A) again and carry it back to (B). Repeat until you have an even number of warp threads lying side by side, all taut and parallel.

Thread the tapestry needle with the weaving thread. Bring it up through the fabric at one end of the warp, close to the first warp thread. Slide the blunt needle under the first warp thread, over the second, under the third, and so on across the full width. Do not pierce the fabric.

At the far edge of the warp, turn and weave back in the opposite sequence: over the threads you went under, and under those you went over. Pull each row down gently so it sits snug against the previous one without puckering the warp threads.

Continue weaving back and forth until the warp threads are fully covered. To taper a leaf shape, drop one warp thread at each end on alternate rows. When weaving is complete, take the weaving thread down through the fabric at the edge and fasten off at the back.

items.symptom: The woven bar is loose and floppy
items.cause: Too few warp threads were laid or they were not held taut.
items.fix: Use at least four to six warp threads laid close together and pulled firmly before starting to weave. Keep the hoop tight so the warp does not shift.

items.symptom: The weaving rows slide apart leaving gaps
items.cause: Too little tension was applied when pulling each row into place, or an odd number of warp threads was used so the alternation breaks.
items.fix: Use the tapestry needle tip to press each completed row down against the previous one before beginning the next. Check that the warp thread count allows clean alternation.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers under the woven bar
items.cause: The needle accidentally pierced the fabric during weaving.
items.fix: A blunt tapestry needle is essential for the weaving pass. If a sharp needle was used, switch to a tapestry needle size 24.
